doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: What sustains him: family, faith and the changed music business
summary: Vega cites his wife, sons with autism, faith, and advice to students on technology, and laments the loss of bandleader mentors like Art Blakey.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: Well speaking of survival, let me wrap up with a question about, you know everybody’s life has ups and downs. Is there something that has sustained you during the low periods in your life?

Well you have to really love what you’re doing. You’ve got to love what you’re doing. And my wife has always been very supportive of me so like when I left private banking she was like, “Good, I’m glad you’re leaving.” Most wives would go, “You bum, what are you doing?” So she was supportive of it. Yeah. I have a supportive family. Look I have two sons that are — I have two adult sons with autism that I have to — that I am their guardian. So that keeps me on track of what I need to do to take care of business. I have to take care of business. At 62 years old I still have to be concerned with taking care of business. I have a spiritual faith system that I’m tied into. Unless folks want to talk to me about it, other than that I just kind of keep it quiet but I believe in the Lord Jesus Christ as the savior of my soul, and he has sustained me through cancer with my son Aaron and through — you know 80 percent of families with parents with autistic kids wind up getting divorced because the stress is just on a whole different level. But so you’ve got to learn to laugh. But as far as what gets me through it I tell my students unless you really love this, if you really want to do this for a living — because I have conversations with them like hey making a living in this is really difficult. It doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do it but what you should do is, as a young person they need to learn all the technology, all the computer stuff, how to record, how to do sessions at home and all that. Because the nature of the business has changed. Nobody is hiring — the whole idea of — I laugh now because people post on social media oh I’m going on a European tour. “How long were you out for?” “Four days.” I’m like going come on man. Man I remember those gigs seven weeks on the road. I would take two suitcases with me because it was rough. You had to take — yeah I remember that. And it wasn’t easy. You know so those things are not really in existence anymore. You know that doesn’t really exist. There is not an Art Blakey out here hiring the next set of young cats to go out and play. Sadly it’s not happening. I think that’s sad. So I think many of my contemporaries who are older have somewhat dropped the ball because they chose to play with their older friends and stop mentoring the next generation of players. Whether that’s a

Maynard Ferguson or an Art Blakey or Horace Silver etcetera. Betty Carter you know. She was out there taking the young bloods and going okay I’m going to teach you about this. So that’s not really happening, but the nature of the business has changed so much. There is no record recording industry. Anybody and their mother can record. Anybody can put their stuff on social media and become a sensation and never have paid any dues.
